people.name: Pierre Bottineau
body: In 1853, when Washington Territory governor Isaac Stevens set out to find a railroad route to the Pacific, he relied on a guide who never learned to read or write but could read the land itself: Pierre Bottineau. Over six feet tall, Bottineau was fluent in French, English, Ojibwe, Cree, Assiniboine, Mandan and Winnebago and could also converse in Dakota. That range of languages made him one of the most sought-after guides of the Upper Midwest.

The Northeaster says Bottineau was born in 1816 at a hunting camp at Bear Point, near the mouth of the Turtle River, close to present-day Grand Forks, North Dakota; a 1902 regional history gives January 1, 1817, near Pembina. His father, Charles Bottineau, was a French Canadian trapper with the North West Company; his mother, Margaret Ah-dik-Songab (Clear Sky), was Ojibwe. He grew up in the Métis world of the Red River, at the heart of the fur trade. In 1830 he made his first long trip as a North West Company messenger, from the Red River to Prairie du Chien.

Bottineau guided families from the Selkirk Settlement to the settlement then called Pig's Eye, later St. Paul. He built a home in St. Paul in 1840, moved to St. Anthony four years later, and donated land for St. Anthony of Padua Church. In 1855 he claimed "Bottineau's Prairie," which became Osseo, and later gave land for Osseo's first Catholic church. During the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 he served as Gen. Henry H. Sibley's chief scout. In 1869 he guided Northern Pacific railway surveyors, and in 1875 he moved to Red Lake Falls, where he founded a town and farmed.

Despite this service he ended life poor; in 1888 a bill in Congress proposed a $50 monthly pension for him. He died on July 26, 1895, near Red Lake Falls. Today a Minneapolis library, a park, a neighborhood, Bottineau Boulevard, and the city and county of Bottineau, North Dakota, carry his name.
keyFacts: 1816 or 1817: Born near the Turtle River or near Pembina; sources differ.
1830: First long trip as a North West Company messenger.
1853: Guides Isaac Stevens's Pacific railroad survey.
1855: Claims the area that becomes Osseo.
1862: Chief scout for Sibley during the U.S.-Dakota War.
1875: Moves to Red Lake Falls.
July 26, 1895: Dies near Red Lake Falls.
people.connectToWork: When someone on your team is the only person who can bridge two languages or two systems, what do they get paid and credited for that work, and who would you turn to if they left?

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Faribault
body: In June 1839 Jean-Baptiste Faribault signed a contract for a three-story stone house at Mendota, built of Platteville limestone and sandstone for $5,000. By then he had spent decades in the river valleys of what would become Minnesota. The house still stands as part of the Historic Sibley Site.

Faribault was born in Berthier, Quebec. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography gives October 19, 1775; MNHS gives 1774. His father, Bartholomew Faribault, had been military secretary to French General Montcalm. At 16 he left school to work as a clerk in a commercial house in Quebec. He joined the North West Company in 1798 and, before 1805, was posted to Little Rapids on the Minnesota (then St. Peter) River.

In 1805 he married Pelagie Kinie Ainsse (also spelled Hanse), daughter of a Frenchman and a Wahpekute Dakota woman, and they raised eight children. In 1819, at the request of Lt. Col. Henry Leavenworth, he moved near the planned Fort Snelling and farmed on Pike Island until floods forced a move; in 1826 he moved his family to the east bank of the river, and by the 1830s they were established at Mendota. He hosted the Catholic missionary Father Lucien Galtier until a chapel was built.
His record also includes harder history. MNHS notes that in May 1833 he purchased an enslaved woman, even though the Missouri Compromise had outlawed slavery in the region.

After Pelagie died in 1847, Faribault moved to the town of Faribault, named for their son Alexander, and died there on August 20, 1860, at the home of his daughter. Faribault County in southern Minnesota is named for him.
keyFacts: 1774 or October 19, 1775: Born in Berthier, Quebec.
1798: Joins the North West Company.
1805: Marries Pelagie Ainsse, of French and Wahpekute Dakota parentage.
1839–1840: Builds stone house at Mendota, now part of the Historic Sibley Site.
August 20, 1860: Dies in Faribault, Minnesota.
Faribault County is named for him.
people.connectToWork: When your program tells its own history, who gets named as a founder, and what would the record look like if it also named the people who were harmed or left out?

people.name: Joseph Nicollet
body: In 1836 a French astronomer travelled alone to the upper Mississippi River to take measurements of the land. Joseph Nicollet would eventually record roughly 90,000 readings of latitude, longitude and altitude across the region. His 1843 map became the first to trace the Mississippi from its source at Lake Itasca to St. Louis.

Nicollet was born in France in July 1786 and trained as an astronomer. He taught mathematics in Paris, becoming professor of mathematics at the Collège Louis-le-Grand, and in 1817 became secretary and librarian at the Paris Observatory, where he studied under Laplace. He lost his fortune in the July Revolution of 1830 and came to the United States to offer his mapping services. After his solo 1836 trip, the U.S. Army's Corps of Topographical Engineers commissioned him to lead an 1838 expedition to the Mississippi's headwaters and an 1839 follow-up on the Missouri River. A young John C. Frémont assisted him on both. In 1838 he also travelled to the pipestone quarry in what is now Pipestone, Minnesota.

Nicollet documented Ojibwe and Dakota cultures, including their names for lakes, rivers and other features, and his use of a barometer was a novelty in American mapmaking. His map, "Hydrographical Basin of the Upper Mississippi River," appeared in a report published in 1843. He died in Washington, D.C., on September 11, 1843, after a long illness, and is buried in the city's Congressional Cemetery. The Linda Hall Library calls it the first accurate map of that part of the country. The National Park Service notes that roads, a city and a county carry his name.
keyFacts: July 1786: Born in France.
1836: Solo expedition to the upper Mississippi.
1838: Leads federal expedition to the headwaters; visits the pipestone quarry.
1839: Missouri River expedition with John C. Frémont.
1843: Dies; his Upper Mississippi map is published.
people.connectToWork: A map or data set can record what local people know and also serve someone else's claim. When your program collects community knowledge, who decides how it gets used?

people.name: Lucien Galtier
body: In 1841 parishioners of a French priest put a three-foot cross on the roof of a new log chapel on the bluffs of the Mississippi and named it "St. Paul." The settlement around it had been known as "Pig's Eye," a name the city narrowly escaped. Lucien Galtier's name for the chapel stuck, and the town became St. Paul, the future capital of Minnesota.

Galtier came from France as one of the seminarians who accompanied Bishop Mathias Loras to the new Diocese of Dubuque. Loras ordained him in his Dubuque cathedral on January 5, 1840, together with Augustin Ravoux and James Causse, and sent him to St. Peter's, the settlement at present-day Mendota across the Minnesota River from Fort Snelling.

At Mendota, fur trader Jean-Baptiste Faribault hosted the young priest until a chapel was built. Because the Mendota church was named for St. Peter, Galtier named the log chapel across the river for St. Paul. That chapel later served as a cathedral, a school and a hospital, and the parish it founded still counts its roots from it.

In 1844 Loras sent him to Keokuk, Iowa, where he built the town's first Catholic church. He was later placed in charge of the parish at Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, where he spent the rest of his life.
keyFacts: 1812: Born in France.
January 5, 1840: Ordained by Bishop Loras in Dubuque, Iowa.
1841: Log chapel named for St. Paul.
1844: Sent to Keokuk, Iowa, where he built its first Catholic church.
1866: Dies at Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin.

people.name: Joseph Rolette
body: In February 1857, both houses of Minnesota's territorial legislature passed a bill to move the capital from St. Paul to St. Peter. Joseph Rolette, chair of the Enrolled Bills Committee, took possession of the bill and disappeared, leaving the legislature to wait through a 123-hour session. Some knew him as "Jolly Joe" for his loud, boisterous personality. The episode is one of Minnesota's best-known political legends, though MNopedia notes that the claim he "saved" the capital is untrue: Judge Rensselaer Nelson later ruled that the removal bill violated the act creating Minnesota Territory.

The legend overshadows Rolette's real importance. He was born October 23, 1820, in Prairie du Chien, son of Jean Joseph Rolette, a French Canadian trader for the American Fur Company, and Jane Fisher. By 1840 he was trading in the Red River Valley for Henry Sibley and Ramsay Crooks, and he rebuilt a trading post at Pembina near the Canadian border. In 1842 he introduced Red River ox carts on trails between Pembina and St. Paul, which drew business from the Hudson's Bay Company and helped make St. Paul the region's commercial hub.

In 1845 he married Angélique Jerome, a Métis woman from Pembina; they had eleven children. Pembina elected him to the territorial legislature in 1851, and he reportedly travelled 18 days by dogsled to reach the capital. By MNopedia's account he served in the territorial House, then the Territorial Council, was a delegate to the 1857 state constitutional convention, and served in the state senate until December 1859. He died at Pembina on May 16, 1871.
keyFacts: October 23, 1820: Born in Prairie du Chien.
1842: Introduces ox-cart trade between Pembina and St. Paul.
1845: Marries Angélique Jerome, a Métis woman of Pembina.
1851: Elected to the territorial legislature.
February 1857: Disappears with the capital-removal bill.
May 16, 1871: Dies at Pembina.

people.name: Pierre Toussaint
body: Today Pierre Toussaint lies beneath the altar of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Manhattan, which the U.S. bishops describe as an honor given to no other layperson. During his life, he was once refused entry to Old St. Patrick's Cathedral because of his race.

Toussaint was born enslaved on June 27, 1766, in Saint-Domingue, the French Caribbean colony that would become Haiti; his grandmother taught him to read and write. The Bérard family, who held him in slavery, brought him to New York when he was in his early twenties, around the time of the Haitian Revolution, and he was apprenticed to a hairdresser. He became one of the city's leading hairdressers, working in the homes of wealthy New York women. After Mr. Bérard died, Toussaint quietly supported Madame Bérard until her death; he was freed shortly before she died in 1807.

In 1811 he married Marie Rose Juliette, whose freedom he had purchased. The couple opened their home to orphans, the sick and anyone in need, and nursed people suffering from yellow fever. St. Patrick's Orphan Asylum was his favorite charity, and he visited it often. By the account of St. Charles Borromeo Church in Brooklyn, he was central to the fundraising for the church on Mulberry Street that became Old St. Patrick's Cathedral and was an important founder of Catholic Charities of New York.

He died on June 30, 1853, and was first buried outside Old St. Patrick's. In 1968 Cardinal Terence Cooke introduced his cause for canonization at the Vatican, and in 1990 his remains were moved to St. Patrick's Cathedral on Fifth Avenue. Pope John Paul II declared him Venerable in 1996.
keyFacts: June 27, 1766: Born enslaved in Saint-Domingue (Haiti).
Early twenties: Brought to New York by the Bérard family.
1807: Freed shortly before Madame Bérard's death.
1811: Marries Juliette.
June 30, 1853: Dies in New York.
1990: Remains moved to St. Patrick's Cathedral.
1996: Declared Venerable.

people.name: Edwidge Danticat
body: Edwidge Danticat's parents left Haiti for Brooklyn when she was a small child: her father when she was two and her mother two years later. She and her brother stayed in Port-au-Prince, in the Bel Air neighborhood, raised by an uncle, the Reverend Joseph N. Dantica, and his wife, until 1981, when at age 12 they joined their parents in Brooklyn. She arrived speaking no English and began in an ESL class. That journey, between languages and between countries, would become the core of her work.

Born in Port-au-Prince in 1969, Danticat studied French literature at Barnard College (B.A. 1990) and creative writing at Brown University (M.F.A. 1993). Her MFA thesis became her first novel, Breath, Eyes, Memory (1994), the story of a girl who leaves Haiti for New York. Oprah Winfrey chose it for her book club in 1998.

Her books range across fiction, memoir and essays, examining dictatorship, migration, family separation and the Haitian diaspora. She has won the American Book Award (1999, for The Farming of Bones), the National Book Critics Circle Award for her memoir Brother, I'm Dying (2007), a MacArthur Fellowship (2009), and the Neustadt International Prize for Literature (2018). In fall 2023 she joined Columbia University as the Wun Tsun Tam Mellon Professor of the Humanities in its Department of African American and African Diaspora Studies.
keyFacts: 1969: Born in Port-au-Prince, Haiti.
1981: Joins her parents in Brooklyn at age 12.
1994: Publishes Breath, Eyes, Memory.
1998: Oprah's Book Club selection.
2009: MacArthur Fellowship.
2018: Neustadt International Prize for Literature.

people.name: Mia Love
body: In November 2014 Mia Love won Utah's 4th Congressional District, defeating Democrat Doug Owens by about 7,500 votes. She became the first Black Republican woman elected to the U.S. House and the first Haitian American elected to Congress.

Love was born Ludmya "Mia" Bourdeau on December 6, 1975, in Brooklyn, New York. Her father, Jean Maxime Bourdeau, fled Haiti, and her mother, Mary Bourdeau, joined him in the U.S. a couple of years later. She moved to Utah, and in 2003 entered politics with a seat on the Saratoga Springs city council. In 2009 she was elected mayor, the first African American woman elected mayor in Utah. She lost her first congressional race in 2012 to Jim Matheson by 768 votes before winning in 2014.

She served two terms, from January 2015 to January 2019, and lost re-election in 2018 to Ben McAdams by fewer than 700 votes. After leaving office she worked as a CNN political commentator. She was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a brain cancer, in March 2022 and received immunotherapy in a clinical trial at Duke University's brain tumor center. She died at her home in Saratoga Springs on March 23, 2025, at age 49.
keyFacts: December 6, 1975: Born in New York City to Haitian immigrant parents.
2003: Elected to Saratoga Springs, Utah, city council.
2009: Elected mayor of Saratoga Springs.
November 2014: Elected to the U.S. House.
2015–2019: Serves two terms.
March 23, 2025: Dies of brain cancer, age 49.

people.name: Dikembe Mutombo
body: In December 2007 a 300-bed hospital opened in Kinshasa named for Biamba Marie Mutombo, who had died in 1997, at 64, when civil unrest closed the streets and kept her from reaching a hospital. Her son, NBA center Dikembe Mutombo, gave $15 million of his own money to the $29 million hospital and research center, a gift announced in 2006.

Mutombo was born June 25, 1966, in Léopoldville (now Kinshasa), in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a country where French is the official language. He came to the U.S. in 1987 on an academic scholarship to Georgetown University as a premed student, expecting to return home as a doctor, but coach John Thompson invited him to try out for the basketball team. Drafted fourth overall by the Denver Nuggets in 1991, he played 18 NBA seasons with six teams. He was an eight-time All-Star and four-time Defensive Player of the Year, and he was inducted into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in 2015. Fans remember the playful finger wag he gave opponents after blocking their shots.

Off the court he created the Dikembe Mutombo Foundation in 1997 to improve daily life in the Congo, and he later served as the NBA's first Global Ambassador. He died of brain cancer in Atlanta on September 30, 2024, at 58.

people.name: Angélique Kidjo
body: In May 2023 King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden presented Angélique Kidjo with the Polar Music Prize, one of the world's top music honors. The singer from Benin had spent four decades carrying the sounds and languages of West Africa to audiences worldwide.

Kidjo was born in 1960 in Cotonou, Benin (then French Dahomey), one of ten children of a Fon father and a Yoruba mother. From age six she performed in a theater troupe run by her mother, and as a teenager she sang with her brothers' band, toured local music festivals and performed on the radio. When Benin's communist regime would not let her work as an independent artist, she left for Paris in 1981, by the Polar Music Prize's account, where she studied at the CIM jazz school and, in 1987, married Jean Hébrail, who composed much of her music. Island Records founder Chris Blackwell signed her in 1991, and they made five albums together over the following seven years.

She sings in Fon, French, Yoruba, Goun and English, and by the time of the prize she had won five Grammy Awards; her fourth, in January 2020, was for Celia, her tribute to Celia Cruz. Beyond music she works for children and women: she has been a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador since the early 2000s, and in 2006, after a trip with UNICEF, she founded the Batonga Foundation, which equips girls and young women with knowledge and skills. She invented the word "batonga" as a schoolgirl, as her answer to people who thought girls should not go to school.
keyFacts: 1960: Born in Cotonou, Benin.
1981: Moves to Paris.

May 23, 2023: Receives the Polar Music Prize in Stockholm.

people.name: Garcelle Beauvais
body: When Garcelle Beauvais arrived in Massachusetts at age seven, she spoke no English and learned it partly from Sesame Street. Kreol Magazine reports that she became the only Black child at her school there. Decades later she would be one of the most recognizable Haitian-born faces on American television.

Beauvais was born on November 26, 1966, in Saint-Marc, Haiti, the seventh and last child of Marie-Claire Beauvais, a nurse, and Axel Jean Pierre, a lawyer. After her parents divorced, her mother brought her and her six older siblings to Massachusetts. After several years at New England boarding schools, the family moved to Miami.

At 17 she went to New York to model and soon signed with the Ford Modeling Agency. She did print work for Avon, Mary Kay and Clairol, walked runways for Calvin Klein and Isaac Mizrahi, and appeared on the covers of Essence and Ebony. Her first television appearance was a mid-1980s episode of Miami Vice, and she had a small role as a rose bearer in Coming to America (1988); she also appears in Coming 2 America.

Her best-known roles include Francesca "Fancy" Monroe on The Jamie Foxx Show (1996–2001) and an assistant district attorney on NYPD Blue (2001–04). She appeared in White House Down (2013) and Spider-Man: Homecoming. She later joined The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills as its first Black cast member and co-hosted the daytime talk show The Real.

She is also an author. Her children's book I Am Mixed, inspired by raising her biracial sons, appeared in 2013, and Amistad, an imprint of HarperCollins, published her memoir Love Me As I Am: My Journey from Haiti to Hollywood to Happiness, written with Nicole E. Smith, in hardcover in 2022 (paperback edition April 2023). It traces her path from childhood in Haiti to adolescence in the Boston area, modeling in New York and acting in Los Angeles.

Age 7: Moves to Massachusetts with her mother and six siblings.

people.name: Roxane Gay
body: A Marvel comic, World of Wakanda, is only one of the many forms Roxane Gay's writing has taken: short stories, novels, essays, a memoir, newspaper opinion columns, a newsletter and a podcast.

Gay was born in Omaha, Nebraska, a first-generation American. Her parents emigrated from Haiti, and in her words they instilled in their children "a profound cultural identity"; she grew up hearing French, English and Creole at home. She attended Phillips Exeter Academy, earned a master's degree at the University of Nebraska, and then a doctorate in rhetoric and technical communication at Michigan Technological University, and spent years teaching creative, professional and technical writing in higher education before Rutgers University–New Brunswick named her its Gloria Steinem Endowed Chair in Media, Culture and Feminist Studies. Her tenure there began in September 2022 with a public conversation with Gloria Steinem; Rutgers' Institute for Women's Leadership lists the term as 2022 to 2026.

Her first book, Ayiti, took its title from the Haitian Creole name for the country. The novel An Untamed State and the essay collection Bad Feminist (2014), a New York Times bestseller, followed, then the story collection Difficult Women, a national bestseller, and Hunger, another New York Times bestseller. Her short fiction has appeared in Best American Short Stories 2012 and Best American Mystery Stories 2014.

As of October 2026 her own site describes her as a contributing opinion writer for the New York Times and the writer of the newsletter The Audacity, and says she once had a podcast, The Roxane Gay Agenda.

Phillips Exeter Academy; M.A., University of Nebraska.
Doctorate in rhetoric and technical communication, Michigan Technological University.
Ayiti: first book, named with the Haitian Creole word for Haiti.
2014: Bad Feminist published; becomes a New York Times bestseller.

people.name: Kwame Raoul
body: In 2004 a vacancy opened in the Illinois Senate when state senator Barack Obama moved on to the U.S. Senate. The man appointed to fill the 13th District seat was Kwame Raoul, a Chicago lawyer and son of Haitian immigrants. Fifteen years later he became Illinois's chief law enforcement officer.

Raoul was born in Chicago on September 30, 1964, to immigrants from Haiti: his father was an internist who practiced in the Woodlawn neighborhood. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science at DePaul University and a law degree from Chicago-Kent College of Law in 1993. He opened a private practice that often represented low-income clients, served as a Cook County prosecutor, worked as a senior attorney for City Colleges of Chicago focused on labor law, and became a partner at two national law firms.

An 11-member committee appointed him to the 13th District seat, and he was sworn in on November 6, 2004. He served 14 years in the state senate, where he was the Senate sponsor of the bill that abolished Illinois's death penalty, passed in January 2011. In 2018 he won election as attorney general, and he was sworn in as Illinois's 42nd Attorney General in January 2019. He took the oath for a second term on January 9, 2023.

As attorney general he has focused on survivors of violent crime, created a task force against organized retail crime networks, and leads the Illinois Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force. His office handles tens of thousands of consumer fraud complaints a year and has pursued industries linked to public health harms, including opioids and e-cigarettes. As of October 2026 he remains attorney general and is seeking a third term in the election on November 3, 2026.
keyFacts: September 30, 1964: Born in Chicago to Haitian immigrant parents.
1993: Law degree from Chicago-Kent College of Law.
November 6, 2004: Sworn in to the Illinois Senate seat vacated by Barack Obama.
January 2011: Senate sponsor of the bill abolishing the death penalty.
January 2019: Sworn in as Illinois's 42nd Attorney General.
January 9, 2023: Takes the oath for a second term.
As of October 2026: Seeking a third term on November 3, 2026.
people.connectToWork: When a person from an immigrant family holds power in your system, what does that change for people still outside it, and what does it leave unchanged?

people.name: Cheick Modibo Diarra
body: When NASA spacecraft headed for Venus, Jupiter and the poles of the Sun, a Malian-born engineer at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory helped calculate how they would get there. Cheick Modibo Diarra joined JPL in Pasadena in 1988 and worked out trajectories for Magellan (Venus), Ulysses (the Sun's poles), Galileo (Jupiter) and Mars Observer, and served as a navigator on the Mars Pathfinder design team.

Diarra was born in 1952 in Nioro du Sahel, in what was then French Sudan and is now Mali, a country where French is the official language. He graduated from Pierre and Marie Curie University in Paris in 1976, then crossed the Atlantic to Howard University in Washington, D.C., where he earned a PhD in mechanical engineering in 1987.

At JPL he later managed education and public outreach for NASA's Mars Exploration Program. In 1998 UNESCO named him its 19th goodwill ambassador to Africa; JPL noted he was the first ambassador born in Africa, the first from the sciences and the first American citizen in the role. His goal was to promote science education in Africa, including a university with a strong science curriculum. In 1999 he created the Pathfinder Foundation for Education and Development, which encourages and supports young African women studying science, including through its Summer Camps of Excellence in Science.

In 2006, after Bill Gates approached him, he became Microsoft's chairman for Africa and the Middle East. After the March 2012 military coup in Mali, he was named prime minister in April 2012 to head a transitional civilian government. Late on December 10, 2012, about 20 soldiers sent by the coup leader, Captain Amadou Sanogo, broke into his residence and arrested him as he prepared to leave for Paris; hours later, on December 11, he announced on the state broadcaster ORTM, "I resign with my government."
keyFacts: 1952: Born in Nioro du Sahel, French Sudan (Mali).
1988: Joins NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
1998: Named UNESCO goodwill ambassador to Africa.
1999: Creates the Pathfinder Foundation for Education and Development.
2006: Becomes Microsoft chairman for Africa and the Middle East.
April–December 2012: Prime minister of Mali's transitional government.
December 11, 2012: Resigns on state television after his arrest the night before.
people.connectToWork: A credential earned in another language or country may not show up the way a U.S. one does. How does your hiring or intake process recognize training and experience that was built elsewhere?

people.name: Josephine Baker
people.field: Performing arts, military intelligence, civil rights
body: In 1963, at the March on Washington, one of the few women allowed to speak told the crowd that she could not get a cup of coffee in an American hotel, "and that made me mad." Josephine Baker had come from France, the country she had chosen as her own, to stand with Martin Luther King Jr.

Baker was born Freda Josephine McDonald on June 3, 1906, in St. Louis, Missouri. After performing in New York during the Harlem Renaissance, she sailed to Paris and opened in 1925 in La Revue nègre at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. She became one of the most famous performers in France, bought the Les Milandes estate in the southwest and moved her family there. In 1937 she married French industrialist Jean Lion, and through that marriage she became a French citizen the same year.

During the German occupation she worked for the Red Cross, entertained troops with the Free French forces in Africa and the Middle East, and worked for the French Resistance, passing secrets she overheard while performing in invisible ink on her sheet music. At the war's end she received the Croix de Guerre and the Legion of Honour with the rosette of the Resistance.

Back in the U.S. she refused to perform for segregated audiences, which usually pushed club owners to integrate, and the NAACP recognized her stand. In France she adopted children of different races and religions, whom she called her "Rainbow Tribe." The common count is 12: Women in World History, at Encyclopedia.com, gives ten boys and two girls, adopted between 1954 and 1965. Sources differ on the details, with Biography.com starting the adoptions in 1950 and the National Women's History Museum counting 13. She died on April 12, 1975. On November 30, 2021, France inducted her into the Panthéon, the first Black woman so honored; her family did not want her body moved from its grave in Monaco, so a cenotaph holding soil from the places she had lived was placed in the Panthéon instead.
keyFacts: June 3, 1906: Born in St. Louis, Missouri.
1925: Opens in La Revue nègre in Paris.
1937: Marries Jean Lion; becomes a naturalized French citizen.
World War II: Works for the French Resistance; awarded the Croix de Guerre and Legion of Honour.
1950s–1960s: Adopts children, most often counted as 12, her "Rainbow Tribe".
1963: Speaks at the March on Washington.
April 12, 1975: Dies.
November 30, 2021: Honored in the Panthéon.
people.connectToWork: Baker refused to perform for segregated audiences, and owners often changed the rule. Where does your own work make a practice of exclusion look normal, and who has the standing to refuse it?

people.name: Soinette Désir
body: Soinette Désir is a Haitian disability rights advocate. Typhoid fever at age 11 left her with a significant disability in one leg. She went to a school in Haiti that was not accessible, where classmates discriminated against her, and she has described being ridiculed in the street.

In 2003 she and a group of other women co-founded l'Union des femmes à mobilité réduite en Haïti (UFMORH), to raise awareness of the rights of women with disabilities and to demand them. She does this through radio and school visits; in 2018, UFMORH worked with six schools. She took part in Equitas' International Human Rights Training Program in 2016 and co-facilitated it in 2018. In 2020 she described herself as UFMORH's coordinator and a human rights trainer.

She has named two problems directly: parents who overprotect disabled children, and violence against women and girls with disabilities. She has also pointed to the gap between Haiti's 2009 ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and real-world access.
keyFacts: Mobility disability in one leg, after typhoid fever at age 11.
2003: Co-founds UFMORH.
2016 and 2018: Participant, then co-facilitator, in Equitas' human rights training.
Focus: girls and young women, who she says face double discrimination, and implementation of the disability rights convention.
people.connectToWork: When a family protects a disabled person, how would you hear from the person directly about what they want, without assuming the family is either the problem or the answer?

people.name: Fenel Bellegarde
body: Fenel Bellegarde is a Haitian disability rights advocate, educator and accessibility strategist. He describes himself as a person with a physical disability. He co-founded the Institut haïtien de langue des signes with two friends, which INSEI describes as the first sign language training organization in Haiti, and he co-created Haiti's first Deaf-centered television program.

He earned a master's degree in accessibility from INSEI in France in 2015, after more than a decade at Haiti's state office for the integration of people with disabilities. Diversability reported in July 2025 that he teaches at Haitian universities and leads the Universal Accessibility Unit in that office. It also says that he worked with Quebec organizations on sign language videos about cholera, launched an e-learning platform, and trained more than 400 young people in Haiti and the diaspora.
He has been honored by the U.S. Embassy in Haiti, Junior Chamber International and the Joël Lorquet Foundation.

2015: Master's degree in accessibility, INSEI, France.
Co-founder of the Institut haïtien de langue des signes.

institutions.name: Alliance Française of Minneapolis–St. Paul
body: In the 1920s a small group led by University of Minnesota professor Jacques Fermand started an Alliance Française chapter in Minnesota, part of a worldwide network founded in Paris in 1883. By the 1950s the chapter had about 100 members. On October 29, 1975, it incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit.

Today the Alliance Française of Minneapolis–St. Paul (AFMSP) serves the Twin Cities and Rochester. It reports more than 1,200 members and over 900 students a year, and calls itself the sixth-largest Alliance in the United States. It offers French classes, cooking classes and summer camps; film groups, concerts and lectures; clubs for high schoolers, book clubs and monthly breakfast conversations; and programs in Minneapolis and St. Paul schools. Its annual Bastille Day celebration and its March Mois de la Francophonie, which features French-speaking cultures beyond France, are signature events.
keyFacts: 1883: Alliance Française founded in Paris.
1920s: Minnesota chapter begun, led by Prof. Jacques Fermand.
1950s: About 100 members.
October 29, 1975: Incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit.
Reports 1,200+ members and 900+ students a year; calls itself the sixth-largest Alliance in the U.S.
institutions.connectToWork: A language school and a language community are not the same thing. If your team needs French, who would you ask to confirm that a person actually wants French, and who would you ask about interpreting quality?

institutions.name: The Haitian Times
body: The Haitian Times began in 1999 as a weekly English-language newspaper in Brooklyn, New York, written for the Haitian diaspora. Garry Pierre-Pierre, who had been planning it for two years, left his reporting job at the New York Times to become its publisher, and Yves Colon, a Miami Herald reporter and editor, took leave to serve as its editor. At launch it was described as the only paper of its kind for Haitian Americans published in English. Publishing in English rather than Creole or French made it readable to second-generation Haitian Americans and to non-Haitian readers, and it describes its readers as opinion-makers and decision-makers in their communities.

Since 2012 it has been online only, which broadened its audience to Haitians around the world. It now reports bureaus in Miami and Port-au-Prince; about 45 percent of its readers are in New York and 35 percent in South Florida, with the rest across the U.S. and abroad. Under the tagline "Bridging the gap," it covers Haiti, immigration, New York, Florida, the Midwest, U.S. politics, arts and culture, sports and business, with a daily newsletter.
keyFacts: 1999: Founded as a weekly English-language paper by publisher Garry Pierre-Pierre (formerly of the New York Times) with editor Yves Colon (on leave from the Miami Herald).
Based in Brooklyn, New York.
2012: Becomes online-only.
Bureaus in Miami and Port-au-Prince; daily newsletter.

institutions.name: Little Haiti Cultural Complex
institutions.type: Municipal cultural center, theater and marketplace
body: In Miami's Little Haiti neighborhood, the City of Miami Parks department runs a cultural complex devoted to Haitian and Caribbean arts. The complex broke ground in 2006, realizing a vision of the late City of Miami Commissioner Arthur E. Teele Jr. It includes a Caribbean Marketplace at 5925 NE 2nd Avenue. On Saturdays local food vendors and artisans set up there to Haitian music. The city says more than 100,000 people a year visit or take part in its programs.

The main complex has a 300-seat proscenium theater, an art gallery showing local Haitian artisans, dance studios for classes such as folk dance, and a courtyard with a mural and stage. It hosts the Sounds of Little Haiti concert series, the Mosaic Marketplace, talks and exhibitions, and a guided neighborhood tour (the Pearl of Miami Little Haiti Tour). Its listed programs include "Sanctuary: Our Sacred Place" and "Crafting With Culture."
keyFacts: 2006: Ground broken, following a vision of Commissioner Arthur E. Teele Jr.
Operated under City of Miami Parks.
Caribbean Marketplace, open Monday–Saturday.

Programs: Sounds of Little Haiti, Mosaic Marketplace, Saturday market.

institutions.name: Union des femmes à mobilité réduite en Haïti (UFMORH)
aliases: L'Union des Femmes à Mobilité Réduite d'Haïti
body: UFMORH (Union for Women with Reduced Mobility in Haiti) is a Haitian nonprofit of women with mobility disabilities. It raises awareness of the rights of women with disabilities and demands them. Its methods include media advocacy, especially radio, and school visits; in 2018 it worked with six schools. It focuses on girls and young women and on implementation of the UN disability rights and women's rights conventions, and in the 2019 protests it provided psychological support.

Soinette Désir and a group of other women founded it in 2003. Esther Louis was its executive director in 2016, when she told the Haiti Funders Conference that "Empowerment must begin in the home." It has been a Disability Rights Fund grantee since 2015. The most recent account we found is from 2020, and we found no Minnesota office.
keyFacts: 2003: Founded by Soinette Désir and other women.
Led by women with disabilities.
Disability Rights Fund grantee since 2015.
2016: Esther Louis, executive director; 2020: Désir, coordinator.

disability.intro:
This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, French-speaking covers very different people: Haitians, who may use Haitian Creole, French or both, and people from West and Central African countries such as Senegal, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea, Mali, Togo, Benin and the Democratic Republic of Congo, who may use French alongside other languages. They differ in faith, region, education and migration history.

We did not find a study of how French-speaking African or Haitian Minnesotans understand disability, and we did not find a Minnesota disability organization focused on them. Community groups that serve French-speaking Minnesotans include the Senegalese Association of Minnesota (since 2009; Wolof classes and immigration help), Diaspora Forces (Togolese and African community, Minneapolis), Vanse (supports Haitian immigrants), Minnesota Accueil (a volunteer network for French speakers, active in 2026), the French-American Heritage Foundation and the Little Canada Historical Society.

What follows comes from small studies of Haitian parents in the U.S., research in Senegal, Cameroon and West Africa rather than among immigrants, and general writing on sub-Saharan Africa.
questions: Which language are you most comfortable using for this conversation: French, Haitian Creole, Wolof, Lingala, another language, or a signed language?
Who gave you or your child a label or diagnosis, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family usually helps make decisions like this, and would you like them here?
What have you been told about why this happened, and what do you yourself think? You do not have to answer this.
Is there anything you are already doing to help, such as prayer, a healer, a church or mosque, or family remedies, that we should know about so the plan fits?
What would you change about this plan?
What goals matter most to you, such as school, work, independence or taking part in your faith?
Would you like us to go over documents out loud, or send a short written summary, and in what language?
Who is it okay for us to share this with?

context.heading: What writers have said about explanations
body: A 2020 article in The Conversation by Baker and Imafidon describes explanations some people hold across sub-Saharan Africa: animist accounts of wrongdoing or witchcraft, and a Christian fatalism that holds disability is God's will. The authors stress that people often combine explanations with medical ones, and that beliefs differ by region, within countries, by type of impairment and by income. It is general commentary, not specific to French-speaking countries.

A 2017 review of research from Cameroon, published from 2005 to 2014, found 46 studies. Knowledge and awareness was the most common theme of its kind (22 studies), followed closely by traditional beliefs (20), and societal attitudes appeared in 21. The authors call it a small body of research. These are research topics in Cameroon. They do not tell you what any person thinks.

sources.label: Baker and Imafidon, The Conversation (June 15, 2020)
Ray, Wallace, Mbuagbaw and Cockburn, Pan African Medical Journal (2017), abstract

context.heading: Family support and a person's own voice
body: A Mastercard Foundation study published in 2023 interviewed 30 young people with disabilities, aged 15 to 35, in urban and rural Senegal. Family support was a strong help, and some family members' negative attitudes were a barrier to school. How much say a young person had depended on their impairment, household and family dynamics, and participants wanted more freedom to make their own choices about school and work.

Many of those 30 young people also reported stigma, including bullying, violence and abuse, and discrimination and exclusion at school and work. The study named misconceptions about disability and a "lack of awareness of the capabilities" of disabled youth among the causes. These findings come from interviews in one study and do not describe any person.

Soinette Désir, of the Haitian organization UFMORH, has named parents' overprotection of disabled children as a problem, and Esther Louis of the same organization told a 2016 conference that "Empowerment must begin in the home." We did not find research on how decisions are shared with elders or extended family in these communities. Ask, and hear the person directly even when family speaks first.

sources.label: Mastercard Foundation and International Centre for Evidence in Disability, Senegal (2023)
Equitas, article on Soinette Désir and UFMORH (July 3, 2018)
Disability Rights Fund, Haiti Funders Conference item (November 17, 2016)

context.heading: Silence is not agreement
body: In a 2010 Florida International University dissertation based on interviews with 10 Haitian parents of children with disabilities in the U.S., the parents seldom disagreed with school staff and did not seem to fully grasp the ways available to raise concerns. Most did not have basic literacy in Creole or English, and they were overwhelmed by written communication from schools. Ten parents cannot describe other families, but the study is a reason to ask what someone would change, offer a follow-up call, and not assume a family reads French or Creole.

sources.label: Gregoire, Florida International University dissertation (2010), abstract

context.heading: Language and words
body: A 2024 study interviewed seven Haitian parents in the U.S. whose children have or had a speech-language disorder. They wanted to keep Haitian Creole, but fear of further language delay shaped their choices. Dropping Creole led to communication breakdowns with family and to parental regret, and the authors call for more education for clinicians about bilingual development. Book an interpreter for the language the person names, not just "French".

For Deaf people, ask which signed language they use. Haiti has its own sign language training institute, co-founded by Fenel Bellegarde, so do not assume that ASL or a spoken-language interpreter will work.

The French sources we read use several terms: personnes handicapées, personnes en situation de handicap, and à mobilité réduite in the name of UFMORH. We found no verified terms in Creole, Wolof or Lingala, respectful or stigmatizing, so none are offered here. Follow each person's own words.

INSEI (France), interview with Fenel Bellegarde
Disability Rights Fund, Needs Assessment of Women and Girls with Disabilities in Francophone West Africa (May 2026)
Equitas, article on Soinette Désir and UFMORH (July 3, 2018)

context.heading: Women and girls with disabilities in West Africa
body: A Disability Rights Fund needs assessment dated May 2026 used questionnaires with more than 450 women and girls with disabilities in nine countries: Mali, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Guinea, Togo, Benin, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire and Niger. Between 70 and 85 percent reported significant difficulty reaching health services, and between 75 and 85 percent reported no stable income. The figures are self-reported, given as ranges and not broken out by country in the summary. They describe the region's systems and do not describe women in Minnesota.

The same report describes strengths: participants' interest in leadership and income-generating work, active organizations of women with disabilities, and growing use of digital tools. The 2023 Senegal study also found compounded discrimination against young women with disabilities.

sources.label: Disability Rights Fund, Needs Assessment of Women and Girls with Disabilities in Francophone West Africa (May 2026)
Mastercard Foundation and International Centre for Evidence in Disability, Senegal (2023)

context.heading: Healers, prayer and formal services
body: Baker and Imafidon cite research on epilepsy in which people were directed to traditional healers rather than medical treatment, and they report that many people combine approaches. We found no Minnesota research on what churches, mosques or Sufi brotherhoods do around disability, so treat that as a question. Ask what the person is already doing, present services as something that can sit alongside it, and raise safety only where a real concern exists.

sources.label: Baker and Imafidon, The Conversation (June 15, 2020)

context.heading: Immigration status and what we could not find
body: We did not find research on immigration-related fears among French-speaking immigrants in Minnesota. That is a gap in the evidence, not a sign that such fears are absent. Sahan Journal (July 2, 2026) reports that the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 25, 2026 to allow Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians to end by the end of July, with no final date set, and Haitian Bridge Alliance also reports the ruling. Sahan Journal estimates about 4,000 Haitians live in Minnesota. The government announced in June 2025 that it was ending the same protection for Cameroon; Sahan Journal said in June 2024 that Cameroonians were then eligible for TPS through June 2025. Check current rules with a legal service, and ask about status only when a program requires it. A policy change says nothing about any one person's status.

We also looked for a Minnesota organization serving French-speaking disabled people and found none. Before reading a missed meeting as cultural, check interpreter booking, shifts, transport and the letters you sent.

organizations.intro: French speakers in Minnesota include immigrants from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Togo, Côte d'Ivoire and other countries, Haitians and Haitian adoptees and their families, and people with French or French Canadian heritage. The Census Bureau counts 16,918 French speakers and 1,914 Haitian Creole speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota for 2020 to 2024, and its 2020 to 2024 birthplace counts include France 1,626, Haiti 1,653, Cameroon 4,077 and Togo 1,731. Census Bureau survey figures reported by Sahan Journal show about 1,400 Minnesotans born in Cameroon in 2016 and about 3,600 in 2022. Those figures count birthplace, not language, and Cameroon has English-speaking and French-speaking regions. Sahan Journal ties the growth partly to the conflict in Cameroon's English-speaking regions, so many Cameroonian Minnesotans may be English speakers. The 2020 to 2024 Census estimate is 4,077 (plus or minus 949). Afoutayi Haitian Dance, Music and Arts Company, which worked with Haitian adoptees and families, says on its site that its activities were moving to Toronto by summer 2026 as its U.S. chapter closed. Diaspora Forces in Minneapolis serves the Togolese and wider African community. We did not find an Ivorian association in Minnesota, a French-language service in a Minnesota congregation, or a local French-language radio or TV program. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.purpose: A statewide coalition of African immigrant communities from 55 countries. It works on business development, education, homeownership, trades and workforce, and it connects local community organizations. It can be a route to groups that do not have their own visible organization.

entries.name: Minnesota Council for Minnesotans of African Heritage
entries.purpose: A state council set in law. It advises the governor and legislature, recommends changes, and serves as a liaison between state government and organizations serving its community. Its own pages are at mn.gov/cmah.

entries.name: Minnesota African Women Coalition
entries.purpose: Describes itself as an African immigrant-led nonprofit working on health equity, mental health and dementia awareness, and small business support. How many of its members speak French is not stated. It filed a federal Form 990 for 2024 on October 25, 2025, but the last events its website lists are from 2024, so check current programs before relying on it. Its site is mnawc.net.

entries.name: Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church
entries.purpose: A parish founded in 1877, when French Canadian representatives and priests bought a former Universalist church so settlers could receive religious instruction in French. MNopedia calls it the oldest continuously used church building in the city. The archdiocese lists its Masses in English only. The same is true of St. Louis, King of France, founded in 1868 for French-speaking Catholics. Both are historic French Canadian parishes rather than current French-language worship sites. Its site is lourdesmpls.org.

entries.name: Mshale
entries.purpose: By MPR News's account in 2022, Minnesota's longest-running newspaper serving African immigrants, founded by Tom Gitaa about 25 years earlier. It publishes at mshale.com.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: A nonprofit newsroom reporting for Minnesota's immigrants and communities of color, free to read. Its coverage includes the Cameroonian community.

entries.name: Fédération des Alliances Françaises USA
entries.location: Bethesda, Maryland, with more than 100 chapters
entries.purpose: Supports local, independent Alliance Française chapters. It offers free online events, and its 2026 convention was in Chicago on October 22 to 25.

entries.name: Haitian Bridge Alliance
entries.type: Immigration advocacy, legal and social services
entries.purpose: Works with Black migrants, Haitians, women, LGBTQIA+ people and survivors of torture. It runs a weekday hotline, offers pro bono legal help by appointment, and litigates on Temporary Protected Status for Haiti.

entries.name: African Communities Together
entries.location: Chapters in New York and in D.C., Maryland and Virginia; none in Minnesota
entries.purpose: Calls itself the nation's largest member-led organization of African immigrants. It works on immigration legal help, housing, economic justice, civic engagement and language access.

entries.name: UndocuBlack Network
entries.purpose: A multigenerational network of Black immigrants that develops member leaders, organizes locally and works on policy.

entries.name: Haitian American Nurses Association International
entries.location: Incorporated in Florida in 2018; chapters include Illinois, Palm Beach, Tampa, Orlando, New Jersey and New York; none found in Minnesota
entries.purpose: A nursing organization for nurses of Haitian descent. A Hudson Valley chapter held a symposium and scholarship gala in September 2026.

entries.name: French-American Chamber of Commerce
entries.location: National network of 17 chapters, including Minneapolis
entries.purpose: A membership network supporting cross-border business between France and the U.S. Listed here as a professional contact, not a human services route.

entries.name: Le Nouvelliste
entries.location: Port-au-Prince, Haiti, in French with an English option
entries.purpose: A Haitian newspaper with daily online news, publishing as of October 2026.

entries.name: France 24
entries.location: Paris, in French, English, Arabic and Spanish
entries.purpose: An international news channel with Africa coverage. The Africascope 2025-2026 survey by Kantar, in the capitals of six countries, found 54.7 percent of residents follow it or RFI each week; that describes those cities, not people in Minnesota.

entries.name: Africanews
entries.purpose: A pan-African news channel publishing as of October 2026.

entries.name: TV5Monde
entries.purpose: International French-language television with the TV5MONDE EDU French-learning service. Africascope 2025, a survey of 11,200 people aged 15 and over in several African countries, reported that 67 percent of 15-to-24-year-olds had watched it in the past 30 days. Its site is tv5monde.com.
entries.linkLabel: Africa Exclusive report on the survey (March 2026)

entries.name: RFI (Radio France Internationale)
entries.location: Paris, in French with African-language services
entries.purpose: International radio, also publishing in Mandenkan and Fulfulde. France Médias Monde reports it first in Libreville and Brazzaville and second in Kinshasa, Abidjan and Yaoundé in the Africascope 2025-2026 survey. Its site is rfi.fr.
entries.linkLabel: France Médias Monde report on the survey

entries.name: Jeune Afrique
entries.purpose: A monthly magazine on African politics and the economy, over 60 years old. Its latest issue is dated October 1, 2026. Its site is jeuneafrique.com.
